archetype.name: Rebuilding (run-first, no pass rush)
archetype.definition: A first-year staff under Jeff Hafley with Malik Willis at quarterback, building around a downhill run game while a defense that cannot rush the passer or get off the field leaves the roster a long way from competing.

report.headline: Run game is finding legs; a rushless pass defense keeps sinking them.
report.take:
Miami is 1-5, and the record matches the play. The Dolphins are 31st in net EPA and 31st in point differential per game, and the point differential implies about 1.5 wins. Wins over expected sit at -0.5, so this is not a team losing coin flips. It is losing on the field, and mostly on one side of it. The offense is below average at 26th in EPA. The defense is close to the worst in football: 29th in EPA allowed, last in success rate allowed and 31st on third downs.

The identity Hafley's staff has built is clear. Miami's pass rate over expected of -10.5 is 31st, so they run far more than the situation calls for. The line has earned some of that trust: first in yards before contact. The flip side is a 26th-ranked stuff rate, so the run game is boom-or-bust. It took off in Weeks 5 and 7 (217 and 156 rushing yards). Willis is the bigger puzzle. The passing game sits at exactly zero EPA per play, and the sacks look like his own doing more than the line's. Miami allows the sixth-lowest QB hit rate, but its sack rate is 27th and it holds the ball longer than anyone. Weeks 4 and 5 produced pass EPA of -12.4 and -11.4, and the Jets win after the bye produced +11.4. That is the range of this offense in one quarterback.

The defensive numbers hide a specific failure rather than a general one. Miami tackles well (eighth in missed-tackle rate) and is a league-average run defense. Yards allowed per game are only 16th. The trouble is that it has six sacks, the fewest in the league, and a 30th-ranked pressure rate. Opposing quarterbacks get clean pockets, and a pass EPA allowed of 0.299 is the result. Offenses go after tight ends and backs: tight ends draw 28.9% of targets against Miami versus a 24% league norm, and the TE1 EPA allowed is the worst in football. This was building before Hafley arrived. The defense was 8th in EPA allowed in 2024 and 25th in 2025, and its current 0.129 matches the 2019 unit that ranked dead last.

Where this goes depends on whether the Week 7 version of Willis is a turning point or one good afternoon. The schedule has soft spots on defense: Detroit and Buffalo twice rank 31st and 32nd, and the Chargers are winless. Those same Lions and Bills offenses rank 3rd and 1st, though, and a defense with no pass rush will not hold them. Special teams also leak about three points of EPA a game. Expect a team that plays some competitive, high-scoring games and wins a few on the ground, but not one that climbs out of the division basement.

strengths.title: A line that creates running room
strengths.body: Miami leads the league in yards before contact, and the staff leans on it with one of the most run-heavy approaches in football. It produced 217 and 156 rushing yards in the last two games, and run EPA turned positive in three of the last four. The 26th-ranked stuff rate means it comes in bursts rather than steady chunks, but the blocking foundation looks real.

strengths.title: Sound tackling, average run defense
strengths.body: Nothing about the defense's failures traces to missed tackles: Miami ranks eighth in missed-tackle rate. Its run EPA allowed sits at 16th. Opponents who try to grind it out get a fair fight, which is why total yards allowed look middling even as efficiency collapses through the air.

concerns.title: No pass rush, no pass defense
concerns.body: Six sacks and a 30th-ranked pressure rate leave the secondary covering forever. The result is a pass EPA allowed among the worst in the league and a 52.1% third-down conversion rate against. This is a personnel problem that has worsened over two seasons, and Willie Gay Jr. and Robert Beal Jr. being out this week does not help.

concerns.title: Willis's sacks are self-inflicted
concerns.body: The line allows one of the lowest QB hit rates in the league, yet Miami's sack rate is 27th and its time to throw ranks first. That points at a quarterback holding the ball rather than protection breaking down. Until that changes, the passing game will swing between disasters like Week 4 and outliers like Week 7.

concerns.title: Special teams bleeding points
concerns.body: At -2.91 EPA a game, Miami's special teams rank 30th. For a team that needs to steal close games, that is a steady hidden cost that compounds the field-position problem the defense already creates.

trend.note: The offense has scored more in each of the last two games than in any of the first four, and Week 7's 28-25 win at the Jets was its first game with positive EPA both passing and rushing. The defense has not improved alongside it, and two games is a thin base.

nextGame.headline: Maye's passing game meets the league's most generous pass defense.
nextGame.body:
New England comes to Miami as a 7.5-point favorite, and the Book has the Dolphins at +310 on the moneyline. The core matchup is ugly. Drake Maye has started every game and New England's pass offense is fifth in EPA, while Miami's pass defense is at the bottom of the league and generates almost no pressure. The Patriots cannot run it, though: their rush EPA is 28th. Their defense is ordinary, 21st against the run, so Miami's ground game is a real lever. New England also gives the ball away more than almost anyone, with a turnover differential 31st per game.

Availability cuts both ways. Miami will be without LB Willie Gay Jr. (a 52%-snap regular) and edge Robert Beal Jr., which thins an already toothless front, and RB Jaylen Wright is questionable with a quad injury. New England is missing CB Carlton Davis III, a 95%-snap starter, which matters against a defense already 31st in EPA allowed to opposing WR1s. Its interior line is depleted, with guard Alijah Vera-Tucker on injured reserve and center Ben Brown out. That is the one spot where even this Miami rush might find a way in.

waysToWin.title: Run at a soft front, shorten the game
waysToWin.body: New England is 21st in rush EPA allowed, and Miami's line has been opening holes for two straight weeks. Long drives on the ground keep Maye on the sideline, which is the best pass defense Miami has. This game script requires staying on schedule early, because the run-heavy plan falls apart when trailing.

waysToWin.title: Malik Washington against a thin secondary
waysToWin.body: Opposing WR1s have feasted on New England by EPA per play, and now Carlton Davis III is out. Washington leads the team in targets by a wide margin. If Willis gets the ball out on time, play-action off the run game aimed at Washington is Miami's best passing look.

waysToWin.title: Cash in New England's giveaways
waysToWin.body: New England's turnover differential is among the worst in the league. Miami's defense has rarely forced turnovers, but against a team this loose with the ball, a couple of short fields could cover for a defense that won't win the down-to-down battle.

waysToLose.title: Maye picks apart a clean pocket
waysToLose.body: A top-five passing offense against a defense with six sacks is the mismatch of the day, and Miami is now missing two front-seven pieces. Expect New England to attack the middle of the field with tight ends and backs, where Miami has been worst. Third downs will tell the story.

waysToLose.title: Willis holds it into sacks and turnovers
waysToLose.body: New England is a top-half sack team. Willis taking sacks and coughing it up turned Weeks 4 and 5 into lost causes. Falling behind early forces Miami off its run plan and into exactly the dropback game where it is weakest.

waysToLose.title: Special teams gives away field position
waysToLose.body: Miami's special teams rank 30th in EPA a game while New England's sit near league average. In a game Miami needs to keep close, that hidden yardage can be the difference.

nextGame.watch: Whether Miami can get any pressure on Maye up the middle against New England's depleted interior line. Without it, the Dolphins' third-down defense is unlikely to get them off the field.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense's recent bump is partly sustainable. The run blocking looks genuine, and Detroit and Buffalo twice bring defenses ranked 31st and 32nd. The passing game's ceiling depends on Willis cutting down the sacks, and his game-to-game variance argues against expecting Week 7 as the norm. The defense is the anchor dragging the season down. A unit with this little pass rush rarely fixes itself in-season, and the back half includes the top-ranked Buffalo offense twice and Detroit's third-ranked unit.

The close-game luck is roughly neutral, so there is no big regression coming in either direction. The soft spots are the Chargers, Colts and Jets games, and that is where the remaining wins probably come from. Expect a top-five draft position fight more than a climb, with scoring a bit better than the first month and points allowed staying high.
swingFactors: Any pass rush emerging from the front seven
Health of the backfield with Wright questionable and Achane in only three games

confidence.note: Six games, but the efficiency rankings sit near the bottom on defense across the board, and the trend matches the 2025 season.
